title: Letting go
hookLine: renunciation as the relief of wanting less, not grim denial

cards: Moving day. The twelfth box comes down the stairs, and inside are chargers for phones nobody in the house has owned in years. The whole box goes in the donation bin, and something odd can happen.
The shoulders come down. The body feels lighter, and not only in the arms. Nobody would call that grim, or a sacrifice.
It's closer to relief. That, in miniature, is the first thought in the Buddha's good pile, and its usual English translation can mislead.

teach.h: NEKKHAMMA: THE THOUGHT OF PUTTING DOWN.
teach.b: The word is nekkhamma, usually translated renunciation, and renunciation sounds like a monk in a cold cell refusing soup. In the suttas the word can point to going forth, leaving home to become a monk or nun.
But it also names a thought anyone can have: the thought of putting something down.
In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, letting go comes first in the good pile, ahead of goodwill and not harming. Here's the honest part.

teach.h: TAPUSSA: IT LOOKS LIKE A CLIFF.
teach.b: In another sutta, a householder named Tapussa tells Ananda that letting go looks, to people like him, like a cliff edge. Ananda takes him to the Buddha, whose answer is candid.

Before his awakening, he says, he too thought renunciation was good, yet his heart didn't leap at it. It only did once he had truly seen the trouble that wanting brings, and tasted the ease of not wanting.
So the tradition doesn't say grit your teeth.

teach.h: LOOK UNTIL THE RELIEF IS REAL.
teach.b: It says look closely until the relief becomes real to you.

The Dhammapada frames it as a trade, in Max Müller's words: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." And nekkhamma isn't only for monks.
Theravada tradition counts it among the perfections, and some lay people practice it in small doses, keeping eight precepts on an observance day.
Less, chosen freely, can feel like more room.

how: Buddhists practice letting go in small doses: on observance days lay people may keep eight precepts, skipping the evening meal and entertainment, and in some Theravada countries men may ordain as monks for a short time.

s: in the suttas, renunciation is only for monks and nuns
it's a kind of thought anyone can have; lay people practice it too, for example on observance days.
the Buddha said letting go always came easily to him
in AN 9.41 he says his heart didn't leap at it until he saw the trouble in wanting.
nekkhamma is one of the ten perfections in Theravada lists
Theravada lists of the pāramīs place it right after giving and virtue.

games.q: you're Tapussa, a householder. you've told Ananda that letting go looks like a cliff edge to you. what does the Buddha say?
o: it's easy; you just aren't trying.
he felt the same, until he saw the trouble in wanting.
games.why: in AN 9.41 the Buddha says that before his awakening his heart didn't leap at renunciation either; it did once he had seen the drawbacks of sensual wanting and tasted the ease of letting go.

practice: Bring to mind one small, live want, the next snack, the reply to a message, a purchase waiting in a cart, and notice how it sits in the body: a lean forward, a little tightness somewhere.
Now, just for these two minutes, put it down; you can pick it up later if you choose. Watch what the body does when you set it down, and if there's any relief, rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Nekkhamma. Letting go, renunciation: the thought of putting something down, first in the good pile, felt as relief rather than loss.

orig.note: Pali nekkhamma (Sanskrit naiṣkramya): letting go, renunciation, from the same family as going forth.

carryVoice: Your line: the relief of less. Letting go can feel like setting down a heavy box. Until tomorrow.
